stages.name: Tax, inequality and the state
stages.title: Tax, inequality and the state
stages.sub: How tax choices change the income gap, and why governments care about closing it.

steps.q: A government raises income tax, which takes a bigger share of pay from high earners than low earners. Is income tax charged directly on a person's earnings, or added onto something they buy?
steps.wrong: Added onto the price of what they buy
steps.hint: Think about whether this tax is taken from wages or paid at the till.

steps.q: The government raises income tax rates on high earners (progressive) and cuts VAT (regressive). Does the gap between rich and poor incomes after tax get wider or narrower?
steps.hint: A progressive tax takes more from the rich; a regressive tax cut helps the poor keep more of what they spend. What happens to the gap?

steps.q: A government swaps some income tax for a higher VAT rate instead. Progressive tax falls, regressive tax rises. What happens to how evenly income is shared after tax?
steps.hint: Less progressive tax and more regressive tax: does this pull incomes closer together or further apart?

steps.q: A country has high measured inequality: some children grow up in low-income households with poor housing and worse health, while others do not. If nothing changes, what is likely to happen to their future earning chances compared with wealthier children?
steps.right: They stay worse off into adulthood
steps.wrong: They catch up regardless over time
steps.hint: Think about what limited income during childhood does to education, health and opportunity later on.
